title: He Could Only Say One Syllable for 21 Years, Yet Understood Every Word
description:
In April 1861 at Bicêtre Hospital in Paris, 51-year-old artisan Louis Victor Leborgne could utter only the single syllable 'tan' despite understanding spoken questions and answering numerical inquiries accurately with his fingers (Broca 1861). Because Pierre Paul Broca preserved Leborgne's brain intact without slicing it, Nina Dronkers and colleagues scanned the 146-year-old specimen with high-resolution 3D MRI in 2007—discovering that permanent speech loss stemmed not just from a surface spot, but from severed deep insula and white-matter fiber highways.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Broca PP (1861 / trans. 2011) Remarks on the Seat of the Faculty of Articulated Language, Following an Observation of Aphemia (Loss of Speech). Neuropsychology Review 21(3): 230-235. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11065-011-9174-x
- Dronkers NF, Plaisant O, Iba-Zizen MT, Cabanis EA (2007) Paul Broca's historic cases: high resolution MR imaging of the brains of Leborgne and Lelong. Brain 130(5): 1432-1441. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/awm042
